title: Scrolls, books and chapters
summary: The Hebrew Bible reckons twenty-four books, not thirty-nine: Samuel, Kings, Chronicles and Ezra–Nehemiah are each one book, and the twelve short prophets share one scroll. The Greek translators split Samuel and Kings into four books of Kingdoms and Chronicles into two, and Latin and English Bibles kept the splits, and printed Hebrew Bibles took them up from Daniel Bomberg's Rabbinic Bible (Venice, 1516–17). Chapters were added in the thirteenth century, verse numbers in the sixteenth.

hebrew.name: Torah
hebrew.summary: Five books, copied on one scroll with four blank lines between each; the Talmud still counts them as five of the twenty-four.

hebrew.name: Samuel
hebrew.summary: One book in Hebrew: Saul's death (1 Samuel 31) runs straight on into David hearing of it (2 Samuel 1). Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, 4QSam-a, copied ≈50 BC, preserves text from both 1 and 2 Samuel on one scroll. The Greek made it the first and second books of Kingdoms, and printed Hebrew Bibles split it from Bomberg's Rabbinic Bible (Venice, 1516–17).

hebrew.name: Ezra
hebrew.summary: One book in Hebrew, called Ezra; the Talmud asks why Nehemiah's words were not given a book of his own name. Origen counts 'Esdras, First and Second in one'. The Greek kept it as one book, Esdras B; Esdras A (the English Bible's 1 Esdras, not its 2 Esdras) is another Greek telling of the return, drawn from the end of Chronicles, Ezra and part of Nehemiah.

overlaps.summary: Chronicles ends with the first words of Cyrus's decree, cut off at 'and may he go up', and Ezra opens with the same words and carries the sentence on: 'may he go to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD'. In the Hebrew order Ezra stands before Chronicles, so the repeated lines join the two books across the scroll's end.
traditions: Ezra wrote his own book and Chronicles' genealogies to his day: the Talmud (Bava Batra 15a)
One work by one writer, 'the Chronicler': Leopold Zunz (1832) and those who followed him
Two works by different hands, the repeated lines a link between them: Sara Japhet (1968), H. G. M. Williamson (1977)

numbering.label: Verses
numbering.summary: Robert Estienne (Stephanus), a Paris printer, numbered the verses of the New Testament in his Greek edition of 1551, printed at Geneva; the numbers were later taken into whole Bibles. The Old Testament's verse divisions are older, part of the Masoretic tradition with the accents that rest on them; numbers for them were first printed in the Latin Bibles of 1528 and 1555, and the Athias Bible (1659–61) was the first Hebrew edition with verse numbers that Jews could use.
